Name: decode_before_check_gap
Title: Refusal Reads the Cipher, Not the Meaning: A Decode-Before-Check Depth Gap Explains Encoding Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Encoding/cipher jailbreaks succeed because of a DEPTH-ORDERING mismatch inside the forward pass: an aligned LLM commits its refusal decision from an early/middle-layer representation that still reflects the SURFACE (encoded) token form, whereas the harmful MEANING of the request is only reconstructed by later layers AFTER decoding completes. The safety check therefore fires 'too early' -- before the decoded harmful semantics are available -- so encoded harmful requests read as benign at the layer where refusal is decided even though a linear harmfulness signal is fully present a few layers deeper. This is stronger and more specific than a generic 'shallow safety' account: it predicts a measurable, signed layer GAP (L_decode > L_check) that WIDENS with encoding difficulty and model scale -- a signature no position-based (TASA) or shallow-alignment account makes, and which explains the paradox that more capable models are more jailbroken. Our primary contribution is this mechanistic ordering finding and its causal test; the training-free Late-Read Refusal defense (re-timing the refusal decision to read the late, post-decode representation) is a secondary, applied consequence.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows cipher/encoding jailbreaks are potent and, crucially, that MORE capable models are MORE jailbroken because decoding ability unlocks harm (CipherChat 2023; Bijection Learning 2024; StructTransform 2025; ObscurePrompt 2024; 'Should LLM Safety Be More Than Refusing Harmful Instructions?' 2025, which splits instruction-refusal from generation-safety on encrypted text). Defenses are input-side (Broken-Token CPT filtering 2025; CIFR probe monitors 2025). Mechanistic safety work locates safety in the template region (TASA 2025), in MLP null-space clustering (What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning 2024), and shows shallow/position-dependent alignment (Incomplete Learning 2025; D-STT 2025). None of these explain encoding jailbreaks as a DEPTH-ORDERING problem — that decoding of the encoded request and the harmfulness check happen at DIFFERENT layers, with the check preceding the decode. This is distinct from my prior lexical-vs-semantic proposal (which decomposes surface tokens vs meaning at a single safety locus in plain text) and from TASA (a token-POSITION account, not a layer-DEPTH/timing account). Our claim is a specific, causally-testable ordering: harmful meaning becomes linearly readable only in later layers than where refusal is committed, and this late emergence is what encoding attacks exploit.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs reliably refuse a plain harmful request yet comply when the same request is encoded (base64, ciphers, learned bijections, structured syntax) -- and, paradoxically, more capable models that decode better are jailbroken more. We propose a simple mechanistic explanation grounded in the geometry of the forward pass: safety and comprehension happen at different DEPTHS, in the wrong order. Specifically, an aligned model commits its refusal decision from a representation at layer L_check that still reflects the encoded SURFACE form, while the decoded harmful MEANING is only reconstructed by later layers L_decode > L_check. The one-sentence delta over the two closest mechanistic baselines is: unlike token-POSITION accounts (TASA) and shallow/position-dependent alignment (Incomplete Learning; D-STT), which say safety lives in specific token positions or shallow layers, we claim a specific layer-DEPTH TIMING order in which harmful meaning becomes linearly readable only AFTER the layer that fixes refusal -- neither baseline predicts the difficulty- and scale-widening gap we test. A surprising prediction unique to our theory: an encoding the model decodes only at its final layer should be MAXIMALLY jailbreaking, whereas a comprehension account predicts the opposite. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, and Gemma-2-9B. First (Location), we track, layer by layer, when the harmfulness of an encoded request becomes linearly decodable (a plain-text harmfulness probe applied across layers, with probe-transfer controls) versus the layer at which the refusal decision is causally determined (layerwise activation patching, block patching, and refusal-logit mediation). We predict a systematic gap that widens for harder encodings and larger models. Second (Causal Intervention), we patch the late post-decode harmfulness component back into the earlier check layer and show refusal is restored, and conversely show ablating late-layer decoding removes harm. Finally we build Late-Read Refusal, a training-free intervention that recomputes the refusal decision from the post-decode representation. The scientific finding is broader than the defense: it predicts that any representation-mismatch obfuscation (not just classical ciphers) that delays meaning past L_check will jailbreak, telling red-teamers where to look and telling model builders that layer-timing of the safety read, not just more refusal training, is the lever. Encoding attacks are operationally relevant (base64/structured-syntax wrappers appear in deployed jailbreak kits), and we restrict all core claims to encodings the model demonstrably decodes.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, plus Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct for the within-family size sweep (the only >9B model; if compute is constrained we drop to the 7B/14B pair only and note the weakened scaling claim). No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal/decode scoring is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we take 40 harmful goals and 40 matched benign requests, and produce 6 encoded variants each at graded decode difficulty: base64, ROT/Caesar, leetspeak, Morse, a learned in-context bijection, and a structured-syntax (SQL/JSON) form -- 40 x 2 x 6 = 480 encoded items plus 80 plain-text originals. For each (model, encoding) we first run a decode-accuracy check on 20 benign encoded prompts and RESTRICT the core analysis to encodings the model decodes >= 80% correctly, since the depth-gap claim only applies where the model CAN decode. Experiment 1 (H1 -- The harmful meaning of an encoded request only becomes linearly readable in later layers): Locates L_decode, the earliest layer at which encoded harmfulness is linearly readable. Data: activations at every layer on the 480 encoded + 80 plain items. Method: train a harmfulness probe on PLAIN-text harmful-vs-harmless activations per layer (difference-in-means + logistic, 70/30 split x 3 seeds), validate held-out AUROC, then apply it across layers to encoded harmful-vs-benign items; L_decode is the earliest layer where encoded-item AUROC crosses 0.7. Cross-check with logit-lens/tuned-lens for where decoded plaintext tokens first surface. Decisive metric first: L_decode per (model, decodable-encoding). Convincing: a well-defined L_decode exists (probe crosses 0.7) for every decodable encoding and sits in the model's later half. Indecision band: peak encoded AUROC 0.6-0.7 -- L_decode ill-defined; reported as a probe-transfer limitation for that encoding. Negative (encoded AUROC never exceeds 0.6 at any layer for a decodable encoding): plain-text harmfulness does not transfer to decoded representations; that encoding is excluded and the transfer caveat reported. Experiment 2 (H1 -- The refusal decision is committed at an earlier layer): Locates L_check, the layer that causally fixes refusal. Data: 40 plain-harmful (refused) and their encoded-harmful (complied) counterparts. Method: layerwise residual-stream activation patching -- patch each layer from the plain-harmful run into the encoded-harmful run and find the earliest layer at which patching flips the output to refusal; that earliest-sufficient layer estimates L_check. Cross-check against attention-to-template loci from prior work. Decisive metric first: L_check per (model, encoding). Convincing: a single earliest-sufficient layer (or a tight 2-3 layer band) reliably flips refusal in >= 2 models. Indecision band: refusal flips only when patching a broad (> 4-layer) contiguous block -- L_check is distributed; we report the block and use its earliest layer by convention. Negative (no single-layer or small-block patch restores refusal): refusal is not localizable this way; the ordering test is reported as inconclusive. Experiment 3 (H1 -- The depth gap: harmful meaning arrives AFTER the check, and widens with difficulty and scale): Tests the core ordering L_decode > L_check and its scaling. Data: the per-(model, encoding) L_decode and L_check from Experiments 1-2, plus plain-text as the reference. Decisive metric first: gap = L_decode - L_check (in layers). Convincing: gap > 0 for all decodable encodings (versus gap <= 0 for plain text), AND gap increases monotonically with encoding difficulty (rank correlation with independently-rated decode difficulty > 0.5) and with model size across the family sweep. Indecision band: gap in {0, 1, 2} layers -- reported as a soft ordering, not a clean gap. Negative (gap <= 0 for decodable encodings, i.e. harmfulness available at or before L_check yet the model still complies): the depth-ordering account is wrong; we report it and pivot to alternative accounts. Experiment 4 (H2 -- Re-injecting the late post-decode signal at the check layer restores refusal): Causal test of the ordering. Data: 60 held-out encoded harmful items. Method: (a) project the L_decode representation onto the plain-text harmfulness direction and patch it into layer L_check; measure restored refusal; (b) reverse control -- ablate the late-layer component that reconstructs plaintext and verify the model neither decodes nor complies; (c) dose-response steering along the harmfulness direction at L_check. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled-label controls; benign encoded items and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of encoded-jailbreak successes converted to refusal by (a). Convincing: >= 50% converted to refusal with monotone dose-response, control directions converting < 10%, and MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% converted -- partial mechanism. Negative (< 20%): the late signal is not causally sufficient at L_check; reported as a null. Experiment 5 (H2 -- Late-Read Refusal defense): Tests whether reading harmfulness at L_decode and gating refusal on it closes encoding jailbreaks at acceptable cost. Data: 480 encoded harmful items (attack-success eval); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item benign-encoded set (legitimate base64/SQL/cipher that must NOT be refused) for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample), MT-Bench (80), and a benign decode-utility check for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model. Systems compared: no defense; Broken-Token input filtering; refusal-direction steering; a CIFR-style activation probe; Late-Read Refusal. Decisive metric first: attack-success-rate reduction across encodings. Convincing: reduces attack success by >= 50% (absolute) averaged over decodable encodings while raising benign-encoded over-refusal <= 5 pp and keeping decode-utility and MMLU within 2 pp (Pareto-beating input filtering). Indecision band: 25-50% reduction or 5-10 pp added over-refusal -- usable but partial; report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 25% reduction or > 10 pp over-refusal or broken decode-utility): the defense does not beat input filtering; reported as such.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The plain-text harmfulness probe may fail to transfer to encoded activations even at late layers if decoded meaning is represented differently than native plaintext; we mitigate by validating the probe fires on model-decoded plaintext and by using logit-lens to confirm plaintext reconstruction, but a probe-transfer failure would blur L_decode. 2) L_check and L_decode may be distributed across several layers rather than sharp points, making the 'gap' a soft ordering; we report distributions and use the earliest-sufficient-layer convention. 3) For encodings the model cannot fully decode, harm may never be reconstructed (a comprehension failure, not a depth-gap failure) — we explicitly restrict the core claim to decodable encodings and treat non-decodable ones as a separate regime. 4) The capability-scaling prediction requires a within-family size sweep; if only limited sizes are available the scaling claim weakens (still, the per-encoding gap is the primary result). 5) Late-Read Refusal risks over-refusing legitimate encoded content (benign base64/SQL/cipher), the key usability trade-off, quantified by the benign-encoded set and Pareto sweep; it could also add a late-layer forward-pass cost. 6) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional; subspace projection may be needed. 7) Directions, L_check/L_decode, and defense strength are model- and encoding-specific and require calibration; adaptive attackers could target encodings whose decode completes only at the final layer, though this constrains the attack and is itself informative.
